title: To engage with AI or not: learning engagement among rural junior high school students in an AI-powered adaptive learning environment
extended_summary:
This study examines what factors shape learning engagement when rural junior high school students use an AI-powered adaptive learning system (ALS). Grounded in self-determination theory, the technology acceptance model, and cognitive load theory, the authors ask how students’ basic psychological needs, technology acceptance, and cognitive load relate to behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and agentic engagement in mathematics learning.

The intervention/context is an AI-powered ALS delivered on tablets during after-school mathematics sessions. The system used diagnostic questions, personalized resource/path recommendations, precision learning, and precision practice, with feedback based on students’ errors and mastery patterns. The study was conducted in five rural junior high schools in southwest China, focusing on seventh-grade mathematics. Students received a week of training on the tablets and AI functions, and a technical staff member was present in classrooms during implementation.

Using a mixed-methods design, the researchers collected questionnaire data from 243 students and conducted interviews with 30 students and 5 mathematics teachers, along with classroom observations. Quantitative analysis showed that perceived competence and technology acceptance significantly predicted learning engagement, while perceived autonomy and relatedness influenced engagement indirectly through technology acceptance. Intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load did not significantly predict engagement in the final model. Qualitative findings supported the importance of usability, personalized feedback, and reducing extraneous load. The paper concludes that AI-powered ALS can support engagement in rural mathematics education, but its effectiveness depends on usability, supportive feedback, and careful instructional design.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational study using survey data, SEM, and some qualitative interviews, but it is not an experiment or randomized design. It provides moderate internal validity for association testing, yet causal claims are limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests engagement-relevant benefits in a priority rural middle-school population, but it does not report direct achievement effects or effect sizes meeting a modest-impact threshold. The observed findings are important for implementation, but the practical magnitude is unclear.

interventions.use_case: AI-powered adaptive learning system on tablets for rural junior high mathematics, using diagnostic questions, knowledge graphs, personalized resource/path recommendations, precision learning, and precision practice with immediate feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centered on grade 7 mathematics use of an AI-powered adaptive learning system, but it does not report direct math achievement gains for this sample. Instead, it focuses on engagement-related antecedents and notes that all participating students used the system for one academic year; prior studies cited in the paper reported higher math scores in ALS groups, but those are not the present paper's findings.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning engagement within AI-powered ALS; no direct achievement test reported in the study results presented here

finding.finding_summary: The core empirical result concerns learning engagement in the AI-powered ALS. Technology acceptance and perceived competence were significant positive predictors of engagement, while perceived autonomy and perceived relatedness were not significant in the revised model; extraneous and intrinsic cognitive load were also not supported as direct predictors. The paper reports SEM/path analysis with n=243, but does not provide standardized coefficients or confidence intervals for the final paths in the excerpted text.
finding.measure: Learning engagement (behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and agentic engagement) and its predictors
